title: Remittance, Tax and NBR Scrutiny When NRBs Buy Property in Bangladesh
metaTitle: NRB Remittance Tax & NBR Scrutiny: Buying Property
metaDescription: How NRBs can fund a Bangladesh property purchase lawfully: banking-channel remittance vs hundi, source-of-fund proof, tax residency and foreign reporting.
keywords: source of fund land purchase Bangladesh
heroIntro: For many Non-Resident Bangladeshis, buying land or a flat at home is a lifetime goal, but the money trail behind that purchase is what tax and financial-intelligence authorities look at first. This pillar guide explains why scrutiny arises at registration, why the banking channel matters, what documents to keep for each way of funding the purchase, and how tax residency and foreign-side reporting fit in. It is written by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on 01712655546.

quickAnswer.heading: NRB Property Purchase: Remittance, Tax and Scrutiny
points: A registered deed records buyer, seller and price, so authorities can ask where the purchase money came from.

Use the formal banking channel and keep every record. Hundi or hawala is unlawful at a high level under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 and can attract the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012.
Keep a source-of-fund file: bank advices, employment and tax proof, gift or sale documents, matched to each payment.
Tax residency depends on days of stay; rates of source tax change with each Finance Act, so check current figures.
Report on the foreign side too, and check current Bangladesh Bank and Authorised Dealer rules before moving money.

sections.h2: Why a Property Purchase Draws Scrutiny at Registration
sections.content:
Buying land, a house or a flat is usually the largest single financial transaction a Non-Resident Bangladeshi (NRB) makes in Bangladesh. It is also one of the very few transactions that leaves a permanent, public, stamped record: the registered deed. Because the deed states the buyer, the seller, the price and the date, it gives tax and financial-intelligence authorities a ready-made starting point for a simple question: where did the money come from?

For a buyer living in Bangladesh, that question is normally answered by tax returns and bank statements. For an NRB, the answer sits partly in another country, in another currency and under another tax system. That is where problems begin. The money may have passed through a friend's account, a family member's account or an exchange house; it may have been sent in several small instalments; or it may have been carried in cash. None of these facts is automatically unlawful, but each one makes the paper trail harder to explain.

This guide is a deeper companion to our general pieces on sending money to Bangladesh legally and the NRB land-buying legal checklist. Its focus is narrow: how to arrange and document the funding of a property purchase so that, if anyone asks, you can answer calmly and completely.

A word on tone. Most NRBs who run into trouble did nothing dishonest. They simply did not keep records, or they used an informal route because it was convenient. The goal here is prevention: build the file before you pay, not after a notice arrives.

sections.h2: Who Can Ask Questions: NBR, BFIU, ACC and Your Bank
sections.content:
Several bodies can have an interest in a property purchase funded from abroad. Their roles are different, and it helps to understand each one at a high level.

  • National Board of Revenue (NBR). The tax authority. It is concerned with whether income has been declared, whether the right tax has been paid at the right time, and whether your assets are consistent with your declared income. Property purchases, bank deposits and other third-party data can be used to test that consistency.
  • Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU). Housed within Bangladesh Bank, BFIU receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and similar information from banks and other reporting institutions, under the anti-money-laundering framework. Large, unusual or poorly explained inflows are the kind of pattern that can generate a report.
  • Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). The ACC has powers to inquire into assets that appear disproportionate to known sources of income, usually in connection with allegations of corruption or abuse of position. It is far less likely to be relevant to an ordinary salaried NRB, but it can become relevant if a purchase is made in the name of, or with money linked to, a public official or politically exposed person.
  • Your own bank. Banks have their own customer due diligence duties. A bank that sees an unusually large credit may ask for the source of funds before it processes a payment order or releases money. That request is routine, not an accusation.
  • Registration offices. The sub-registrar checks the deed, the price against the applicable minimum value and the payment of government charges. Information from registration offices and banks can be shared with the tax authority under the rules in force at the time.

Two practical points follow. First, you will not always meet these bodies at the same moment. A purchase made today may be queried years later during a tax assessment, an audit or a dispute with a seller or relative. Second, the burden of explaining the funds usually falls on the person who owns the asset. Records are therefore your protection, and they should be kept for the long term.

sections.h2: Banking-Channel Remittance vs Hundi or Hawala
sections.content:
The single most important decision you make is how the money travels. In Bangladesh the lawful route is the formal banking channel: money sent through a bank, an authorised exchange house or a licensed mobile financial service arrangement that credits a bank account in Bangladesh with a traceable record.

Hundi (also called hawala) is an informal value-transfer system. Typically you hand local currency to an agent abroad, and a counterpart in Bangladesh pays taka to your relative or to the seller, with no money formally crossing the border. It can look cheaper and faster, and the rate offered is sometimes better. It is also, at a high level, unlawful in Bangladesh: dealing in foreign exchange outside authorised channels is prohibited under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, and moving or concealing funds of unclear origin can attract the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012. Penalties under these laws can include imprisonment and forfeiture, and the offence can sit with the person who uses the route as well as the agent who runs it.

Beyond the legal risk, hundi has a practical cost that NRBs rarely consider until later: it produces no paper. There is no bank advice, no remittance record, no evidence that the taka in the seller's hands came from your foreign earnings. If a question is ever asked, you may have nothing to show. Money received informally also cannot be easily claimed as lawful inward remittance when you want to document the purchase, and it may complicate any later wish to repatriate sale proceeds.

A banking-channel remittance, by contrast, creates a chain of documents: your foreign bank debit, the transfer instruction, the intermediary or exchange-house record, and the credit advice in Bangladesh. Where your Bangladesh bank issues a remittance or encashment advice, ask for it and keep it. Whether a particular certificate is issued, and what it is called, depends on the bank and current practice, so ask your Authorised Dealer bank what proof it provides.

If you have already used an informal channel in the past, do not try to hide it or paper over it with invented documents. Get advice before you make any statement to an authority. Forged or back-dated documents turn a manageable explanation problem into a criminal one.

sections.h2: Bangladesh Bank Rules for Buying Property with Foreign Currency
sections.content:
Foreign-exchange control in Bangladesh is administered by Bangladesh Bank through its Foreign Exchange Regulation framework and circulars issued to Authorised Dealer (AD) banks. These rules are detailed and are updated from time to time. Always check the current Bangladesh Bank and Authorised Dealer rules before you move money. The points below are a high-level orientation, not a substitute for that check.

  • Use an Authorised Dealer bank. Inward remittances should reach your Bangladesh account through an AD bank or an approved channel so that the inflow is recorded as a foreign-exchange receipt.
  • Foreign-currency accounts. NRBs may be able to hold foreign-currency accounts in Bangladesh, commonly referred to as NFCD (Non-Resident Foreign Currency Deposit) accounts, and residents may hold RFCD (Resident Foreign Currency Deposit) accounts under defined conditions. Who is eligible, what can be credited and how the balance can be used for a property purchase are matters governed by current circulars. Do not assume that money in such an account can be paid directly to a seller; ask your bank to confirm in writing.
  • Purpose of remittance. Banks often ask you to state the purpose of an inward transfer. Choose the purpose that is truthful. A transfer labelled as family support but used to pay a land seller creates an inconsistency that you may later have to explain.
  • Payment to the seller. In most transactions, the price should be paid by an account-payee instrument or bank transfer that appears on the deed or in a payment schedule, not in cash. Cash payments of large amounts are hard to prove and invite questions.
  • Foreign nationals and dual citizens. The rules on who may buy property depend on citizenship status. If you hold a foreign passport, read our guide on foreigners and dual citizens owning property first, because your status affects both the permission to buy and the exchange-control treatment of the funds.

If a bank officer gives you an oral answer about what is permitted, ask for it in writing or by email on bank letterhead. Policies are interpreted differently across branches, and a written confirmation is much better evidence of good faith than a conversation.

sections.h2: Tax Residency and NRB Status for Income Tax
sections.content:
"NRB" is a practical label; for income tax what matters is tax residency, which is determined by the law for each income year, not by your passport or your intention. In general terms, residency under Bangladeshi tax law depends on the number of days you were physically present in Bangladesh in the income year, with a basic threshold of about half a year and additional tests that look at earlier years. The exact thresholds and wording are set out in the Income Tax Act 2023 and can be amended, so check the current text or ask a tax professional.

Why does this matter?

  • A non-resident is generally taxed in Bangladesh on income that arises, accrues or is received in Bangladesh, not on income earned and kept abroad.
  • A resident is generally taxed on worldwide income, which can include foreign salary, foreign rent and foreign investment returns, subject to any relief for foreign tax paid.

An NRB who returns to Bangladesh for long periods, for example to supervise construction, may unintentionally cross the threshold and become a tax resident for that year. Keep a simple travel log from your passport stamps, boarding passes and e-gate records. It is the cheapest piece of evidence you will ever create, and it is exactly what an assessing officer will ask for when deciding which category you fall in.

Residency also interacts with foreign tax law. You may be a tax resident of the UK, the USA, Canada, the UAE or another country for that country's purposes while being a non-resident for Bangladesh. The two tests are independent. Do not assume that being "non-resident" in one place answers the question in the other.

Finally, status can change from year to year. A year spent largely in Bangladesh may be treated differently from the years either side of it, so review your position annually rather than relying on a past conclusion.

sections.h2: Source Tax, Wealth Statement and Disclosure at Registration
sections.content:
When a deed is registered, several government charges and advance taxes are collected on the transaction. These typically include stamp duty, registration fee, local government tax and a tax collected at source in connection with the transfer, along with other charges depending on the location and type of property. The rates and the way they are calculated are set by law and are often changed by the Finance Act or by NBR orders each year, so we do not quote numbers here. Your deed writer or lawyer should obtain the current schedule from the sub-registry office, and our separate registry cost guide (in Bengali) explains the cost heads in more detail.

It is important to understand a point many buyers miss: paying source tax at registration does not, by itself, settle your tax position. It is generally an advance or adjustable amount, and it does not prove that the money used for the purchase was lawfully earned or properly declared. Those are separate questions.

Disclosure of the asset itself is dealt with through your income tax return. Where you are required to file a return and the law requires a statement of assets and liabilities (often called a wealth statement), a newly bought property should appear in it, with its acquisition cost and the source of funds. If you are tax-resident in Bangladesh, or if you have Bangladesh-source income that brings you into the return system, check whether the asset statement is required for you. The thresholds and forms are updated regularly, so verify them for the current assessment year.

If you are not required to file a Bangladesh return, you should still keep the full source-of-fund file described below. A person who is outside the return system may be asked to explain a purchase if a notice is issued or an enquiry is opened. For a related discussion of notices triggered after land transactions, see our Bengali article on tax notices after buying and selling land.

Finally, remember that the declared deed value, the actual price paid and the amount shown as remitted should tell the same story. Large gaps between them are a common reason for follow-up questions.

sections.h2: Documents to Keep for Each Funding Route
sections.content:
Your documentary needs depend on how the money reached the seller. The table below summarises the usual file for each route, the purpose it serves and the typical risk if the proof is missing. It is a guide, not an exhaustive list, and your bank or adviser may ask for more.

Funding routePurpose of the documentTypical proof to keepRisk if missing
Banking-channel remittanceShows the funds entered Bangladesh lawfully and are traceable to you.Foreign bank statement showing the debit; transfer instruction or receipt; Bangladesh bank credit advice; remittance or encashment advice if your bank issues one; your account statement showing the credit and onward payment.Cannot link your foreign earnings to the taka paid; weak answer to a source-of-fund query.
Wage-earner remittance (salary sent home)Connects the remittance to a real job and real income abroad.Employment contract or letter; payslips; foreign tax return or tax statement; work permit or residence permit; monthly bank statements showing salary and transfers.Remittance looks unexplained or out of proportion to declared income; inconsistent purpose statements.
Foreign-currency account (NFCD/RFCD)Shows the balance came from lawful foreign-currency sources and was used within the account rules.Account opening documents; deposit records and their origin; bank written confirmation that the balance may be used for the purchase; statements showing conversion and payment.Bank refuses the payment or the use of funds is questioned; origin of deposits cannot be shown.
Gift from relativesShows a genuine gift and that the donor had lawful funds.Signed gift letter naming donor, recipient and amount; donor identity and relationship proof; donor bank statement; evidence of donor source of funds; proof of transfer through a banking channel; tax treatment note from an adviser.Treated as unexplained money; donor funds themselves may be questioned; possible gift or tax issues on either side.
Sale of a foreign assetShows the funds came from a documented disposal abroad.Sale contract; completion statement or closing statement; evidence of title and prior purchase; foreign tax filing for the gain, if any; bank statement showing proceeds received; transfer records to Bangladesh.Source looks undocumented; foreign tax may be unpaid; difficulty proving the amount and timing.
Mixed funding (for example, savings plus a family loan)Shows each part separately.A reconciliation sheet listing each amount, its source and its proof; loan agreement and repayment plan; matching bank records.One weak part can contaminate the whole file; the totals do not match the price.

Whatever the route, keep both the original documents and clean scanned copies. If a document is in a foreign language, keep a certified translation. Documents from abroad that you intend to use formally in Bangladesh may require attestation or legalisation, so ask early.

Use this sequence from the moment you decide to buy. It is designed so that each payment can be traced from your foreign income to the seller's receipt.

  1. Decide your status. Confirm whether you are a Bangladeshi citizen, a dual citizen or a foreign national, and keep proof such as passport, NVR endorsement or NID. This affects what you may buy and how funds are treated.
  2. Open or confirm the right bank account. Speak to an Authorised Dealer bank branch about the account type, and ask in writing what the bank needs for inward funds meant for a property purchase.
  3. Build a source-of-fund file before you send anything. Gather employment proof, payslips, foreign tax returns, savings statements and any sale or gift documents, matched to the amounts you plan to send.
  4. Send money only through banking channels. Avoid cash, third-party accounts and informal agents. State the true purpose of each transfer.
  5. Keep every transfer document. Retain the foreign debit record, transfer receipt and Bangladesh credit advice for each instalment, and note the exchange rate used.
  6. Verify the property and seller. Do title checks, khatian and mutation history and any pending dispute before paying. Our guide on buying land from abroad sets out the legal checks.
  7. Pay the seller by traceable means. Use account-payee cheque or bank transfer, record each payment, and make sure the paid amount matches the deed and the payment receipts.
  8. Pay government charges through the official channel. Keep the challans, payment orders and receipts for the stamp duty, registration fee and taxes collected at registration.
  9. Register the deed and collect the certified copy. Check the price, party details and schedule on the deed before leaving the office.
  10. Complete mutation. Apply for mutation so the record shows your name. See land mutation (namjari) from abroad.
  11. Update tax records. Include the asset in any return or asset statement that applies to you in Bangladesh, and discuss your foreign-side reporting with a tax professional in the country where you are resident.
  12. Archive the file. Create one folder, physical and digital, with an index. Keep it for as long as you own the property and for a long period after any sale, since tax questions can arise years later.

sections.h2: Double Taxation Treaties and Foreign-Side Reporting
sections.content:
Bangladesh has entered into double taxation avoidance agreements (DTAs) with a number of countries. A treaty may allocate taxing rights between the two states, provide a method for relief or credit for tax paid in the other country, and set out rules for resolving residency conflicts. Whether a treaty exists between Bangladesh and your country of residence, and what it says about the type of income you have, must be checked individually. A treaty never removes the duty to file or to disclose; it only reduces the risk of being taxed twice on the same income.

Equally important is reporting in the country where you live. Many countries require residents and citizens to report foreign assets and foreign accounts, even where no tax is due. Examples that NRBs commonly meet include:

  • United States: reporting of foreign financial accounts (FBAR) and foreign financial assets under FATCA rules, which may be relevant if you are a US person.
  • United Kingdom: disclosure of overseas income and gains through the self-assessment system administered by HMRC, and rules on residence and domicile or its replacement concepts.
  • Canada, Australia, the Gulf states and others: each has its own regime on foreign income, foreign property and bank accounts.

Failure to report on the foreign side can be penalised heavily, and information is increasingly exchanged between tax authorities under international reporting standards. A purchase that is perfectly tidy in Bangladesh can still create a problem abroad if it is never mentioned. We are Bangladesh-law advisers and do not advise on foreign tax. Please engage a qualified tax professional in your country of residence, and ask them to coordinate with a Bangladeshi adviser so that the two filings are consistent in amounts, dates and exchange rates.

sections.h2: Repatriating Sale Proceeds: A High-Level View
sections.content:
Many NRBs ask at the time of buying whether they can later take the money back out. The honest answer is that it depends on your status, on how the purchase was funded and on the Bangladesh Bank rules in force at the time of sale. In general, outward remittance of sale proceeds is controlled, and the ability to repatriate is far stronger when you can prove two things: that the original purchase was funded by lawful inward remittance, and that the relevant taxes were paid on both the purchase and the sale.

That is one more reason to use the banking channel. An NRB whose purchase was funded through documented inward remittance is in a much better position to apply for approval to remit proceeds than one whose money arrived informally and cannot be traced. Any approval, conditions and limits are matters for Bangladesh Bank and your Authorised Dealer bank, so check the current requirements and, if the sum is large, take advice before the sale rather than after.

Sale itself carries tax consequences: the seller's side may involve tax at the time of transfer and capital gain or other income tax rules. Those depend on the holding period, the type of asset and the current law. Plan the sale paperwork with the same discipline as the purchase: sale deed, payment records, tax payment proof and a clear trail from the buyer's money to your account.

• Using hundi because it is convenient. The saving is small compared with the legal exposure and the loss of documentary proof.
  • Sending money through a relative's account without a record. If the relative then pays the seller, your link to the funds depends on informal understanding. Use a written gift or authority letter and keep bank evidence.
  • Structuring payments into small amounts to avoid attention. Splitting transfers to stay under a notional limit can itself look suspicious and may attract reports.
  • Understating the deed value. Declaring a lower price to reduce charges creates a gap between the deed and the money trail, with consequences for both the buyer and the seller. The deed value must also respect the applicable minimum value.
  • Paying part in cash. Cash cannot be traced. If a seller insists on cash, treat it as a warning sign.
  • Giving a false or vague purpose to the bank. A remittance labelled with an untrue purpose will not match later documents.
  • Ignoring tax residency. Spending long periods in Bangladesh without tracking days may change your status for the year.
  • Forgetting the foreign-side filing. A Bangladesh purchase may need disclosure abroad.
  • Relying on a power of attorney without safeguards. If an agent handles payments and registration for you, make sure every payment still passes through your documented channel.
  • Throwing records away. Tax questions can be raised long after the purchase. Keep records for the life of the asset.
  • Creating documents after the fact. Back-dated gift letters or invented receipts can lead to criminal liability for forgery. If something is missing, obtain a genuine replacement from the bank or counterparty.

sections.h2: What to Do If You Receive a Notice or Query
sections.content:
If a tax office, bank or other authority sends you a notice asking about the source of funds for a property purchase, do not panic and do not ignore it. A notice is a request for information; it is not a finding that you did anything wrong.

  1. Read the notice carefully. Note the issuing office, the legal provision cited, the property or transaction mentioned and the deadline.
  2. Do not miss the deadline. If you need more time, ask for it in writing before the date passes.
  3. Collect your file. Use the table and checklist above to assemble remittance advices, statements and supporting documents.
  4. Prepare a short chronology. One page showing dates, amounts, sources and payments is more persuasive than a pile of papers.
  5. Respond in writing and keep proof of delivery. Do not give oral assurances you cannot support with documents.
  6. Take advice before admitting anything. A lawyer and tax adviser can help you frame the response and, where necessary, correct a past position properly.

If your difficulty is a land dispute, a missing record or a question about mutation rather than tax, you may also want to read the broader material in our NRB legal help hub.

Cross-border purchases combine exchange-control law, anti-money-laundering rules, income tax law, registration law and foreign tax law. No single article can cover your exact facts. The most protective steps are consistent and simple: use the banking channel, tell the truth about the purpose and amount, keep a complete source-of-fund file, pay the government charges officially, and report on both sides of the border.

For more on lawful transfers, see our guide to sending money to Bangladesh legally, and for the overall NRB library visit the NRB legal help hub.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms, tax rates and procedures change, often with each annual Finance Act or Bangladesh Bank circular; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate and tax professional before acting.

faqs.question: Why does the tax office ask about my source of funds when I buy property?
faqs.answer: A registered deed is a permanent record of a high-value transaction. Tax authorities use such records to check whether declared income can reasonably explain an asset. For an NRB, the explanation usually sits partly abroad, so documentary proof of the foreign income and the remittance trail matters.

faqs.question: Is hundi or hawala illegal in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: At a high level, yes. Dealing in foreign exchange outside authorised channels is prohibited under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, and moving funds of unclear origin can attract the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012. Use banks and authorised exchange houses instead.

faqs.question: What proof should I keep for a banking-channel remittance?
faqs.answer: Keep your foreign bank debit record, the transfer receipt, the Bangladesh bank credit advice, any remittance or encashment advice your bank issues, and statements showing the onward payment to the seller. Ask your Authorised Dealer bank which documents it provides.

faqs.question: Can I use money in a foreign-currency (NFCD or RFCD) account to buy property?
faqs.answer: It may be possible, but it depends on the current Bangladesh Bank and Authorised Dealer rules and on your status. Ask your bank to confirm in writing how the balance may be used before you proceed.

faqs.question: Can a relative gift me the money for a property purchase?
faqs.answer: A gift can be legitimate, but it needs a signed gift letter, proof of relationship, evidence of the donor's lawful source of funds and a banking-channel transfer. There may also be tax consequences on either side, so take advice.

faqs.question: Does paying tax at registration mean my source of funds is accepted?
faqs.answer: No. Source tax and other charges collected at registration are separate from the question of whether the money used was lawfully earned and properly declared. Keep your source-of-fund file regardless.

faqs.question: How is an NRB treated for income tax in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: It depends on tax residency, which is generally determined by days of physical presence in the income year under the current law, not by passport. A non-resident is generally taxed on Bangladesh-source income. Check the current Income Tax Act 2023 thresholds or consult a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I need to report my Bangladesh property in the country where I live?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Many countries require residents to report foreign assets or income, and some exchange information with other tax authorities. Speak to a qualified tax professional in your country of residence.

faqs.question: Can I take the sale proceeds of my Bangladesh property back abroad?
faqs.answer: Outward remittance of sale proceeds is controlled and depends on your status, how the purchase was funded and current Bangladesh Bank rules. Documented inward remittance and proof of tax payments make approval easier. Check the current requirements before selling.
